Ancient Teyvat Script (also: Abyss Language, Abyssal script, Abyssal letters, Khaenri'ahn alphabet): The Ancient Teyvat Script is the community name for the Latin-based lettering that appears on seals, Ley Line monoliths, domain walls, magic circles, ruins and the gear of the Abyss Order. The game never names it. It is separate from the common Teyvat Script that ordinary people write in, and context ties it to the Unified Civilization of 6,000 years ago and to Khaenri'ah.

Practice: The script has no capital letters and, in most texts, no spaces. It mostly appears as short ritual phrases, labels or mottos rather than flowing prose, and is associated with magic seals, gods, alchemy, astrology and Ley Lines.

1.content:
Hilichurlian (also: Hilichurl language, hilichurl speech, Hilichurlian Linguistics, Hilifolk): Hilichurlian is the language of the hilichurls, the masked tribal creatures found across Teyvat. It is made of short, often repeated words, strongly tied to feelings, food, fighting and song. Almost nobody studies it: the scholar Ella Musk of Mondstadt and her ancestor Jacob Musk are the main authorities. Ordinary people assume hilichurls cannot communicate at all, and hilichurls attack most outsiders on sight, but a visitor who uses the right words can be answered with a dance instead of a club.

Practice: Hilichurls speak in clipped words and repeat them for emphasis. Common examples the handbook records: da or dada (good, very), muhe (like or want), ika ya (a bad person), mita (meat, liked things), gusha (plants, disliked things), celi (hot, fire, sometimes the sun), lata (cold) and unu (one, and the word tied to their sense of the divine). Mosi mita and mosi gusha work as figures of speech for happiness and sadness.

Scene use: Hilichurls rarely hold conversation. A short phrase, a gesture and a mood do most of the work. A visitor who speaks even a few friendly words (offering food, calling dada, saying odomu for friend) may calm a camp; one wrong word, especially an insult like ika, ends in a fight.

2.content:
Hot Pot Game (also: hotpot game, God of Hot Pot's blessing): The Hot Pot Game is a light guessing game played at a hot pot meal. Each person secretly adds one ingredient to the shared pot. Players then take turns closing their eyes, fishing out and tasting an ingredient, and guessing whose it was. It is played for laughs among friends, and the stakes are small.

Practice: Rules as Thoma gives them: everyone prepares an ingredient and the ingredients all go into the pot when the meal begins. Players take turns to close their eyes, pick something out, taste it and name its owner. A correct guess earns a point and another turn. The player with the most points when the pot is finished wins.

3.content:
Martial Arts in Teyvat (also: Teyvat martial arts, martial arts schools of Teyvat): Teyvat's martial arts are named fighting schools, each tied to a place, a clan or a founder, and each usually built around particular weapons. Mondstadt's Knights of Favonius teach Favonius Bladework with sword and claymore. Liyue favours swords and polearms, with the Guhua Clan's arts, the yaksha's demon-slaying dance, the Wangsheng spear arts and Yunlai Swordsmanship. Inazuma has the most formally named schools: Iwakura, Kitain, Kamisato, Kaedehara, Meikyou Shisui, Kujirai, Shinryuu and the Raiden Shogun's Origin. Natlan is known for boxing, and Khaenri'ah's Black Serpent Knights had their own bladework.

Practice: Schools are built around a weapon or technique, handed from founder to students, and often kept alive by one clan or dojo. Masters, rivals and duels are normal parts of the world, especially in Inazuma.

4.content:
Medicine in Teyvat (also: Teyvat medicine, medicine and healing in Teyvat, Teyvat healthcare): Medicine in Teyvat is a patchwork rather than one system. Herbal remedies are the everyday base, sold by pharmacists and herbalists, most famously at Liyue's Bubu Pharmacy. Sumeru runs an Akademiya hospital, the Bimarstan, offering free care. Surgery, therapy and medication all exist. Elemental power is also used for healing, Hydro and Anemo most visibly: Barbara and Jean are known healers. Practice differs a great deal between nations.

Practice: Common treatments are plant-based: bitter herbs, teas, balms and brews prepared to a prescription. Minor injuries get bandages and wound dressings; dislocations are set by hand. Healers with elemental power can mend injuries directly.

5.content:
Naming Conventions of Teyvat (also: Teyvat names, naming conventions, Teyvat naming, names in Teyvat, family names in Teyvat): Names in Teyvat vary by nation and mostly reflect regional flavour: Mondstadt names sound German, Liyue names are Chinese-style, Inazuma places clan first, Fontaine names are French, and Natlan has the Ancient Name, an inherited title that is also a stone. In scenes, keep each nation's names consistent and avoid mixing styles inside one family.

Practice: Use each nation's naming style for new characters; use titles and clan names as the world does; and never assume everyone has a family name.

Scene use: Introduce a new Inazuman with the clan name first, a Natlan character possibly with an Ancient Name, and a Fatui agent with an Italian title. Do not give an in-world explanation for why the names look the way they do.

6.content:
Symbols in Teyvat (also: Teyvat symbols, Teyvat motifs, triquetra, triskelion, Solomon's knot, four-pointed star, Palestar, pale star): Teyvat has a handful of shared visual motifs that recur across nations: the triquetra (on the Mora and Domain doors), Solomon's knot, the triskelion, a four-pointed star tied to Primogems and the Traveler, and a Celestia-linked "celestial" motif. Each nation and many organisations also carry their own heraldry, such as the Knights of Favonius crest, the Akademiya emblem and the Fatui's Palestar. Canon rarely explains what the shared symbols mean.

Practice: Shared motifs appear on currency, doors, ruins, clothing and gadgets rather than being taught or explained. Organisations use crests to mark membership: on uniforms, hats, scarves, masks and banners.

Regional variation: Each nation has local heraldry, and Character Cards use national ornament to show affiliation.

7.content:
Teyvat Script and Common Tongue (also: Teyvat Script, Teyvat Language, common script, common language of Teyvat, common tongue): The Teyvat Script is the common writing seen across most of the world: on signposts, shop signs, books, notices and tutorial pages. It is the everyday way to write the common language that most people in Teyvat speak. "Teyvat Script" is an unofficial name; in the world, people simply read and write.

Practice: Characters read signs and notices as plain words. Nobody comments on the lettering. Letters, notes and menus in scenes can be treated as ordinary written language.

Scene use: Do not mention fonts or mirror-writing. A character who is literate reads the sign. Use the common tongue as the default language of scenes between people from different nations.

8.content:
Unu (also: Unu (Hilichurlian), hilichurl holy word, hilichurl concept of gods): Unu is a Hilichurlian word. The Handy Handbook of Hilichurlian calls it a holy word that embodies the hilichurls' idea of gods and the origin of life. The same word also means "one." Canon gives no name, shape or personality for any single god behind it, so portray it as a reverent word, not a character.

Practice: Unu appears in hilichurl song. Jacob Musk's Hilichurl Ballad Selection records a pious ode, built on repeated cries of "unu, unu," that hilichurls sing only during sacrifices. Hilichurls seem to beat the weakest tribe members with planks as percussion during it.
